newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Wheat shortage mars Moslem feast in Pakistan.
newsitem.headline: Wheat shortage mars Moslem feast in Pakistan.

text.p: Thousands of people jostled in bread queues in Pakistan's southern city of Karachi on Friday, dampening the usually joyful Moslem Eid al-Adha festival, witnesses said.
Tempers were running high as long queues of men and children formed at roadside bakeries for flat loaves of bread under the watchful eye of police and paramilitary rangers, they said.
There were no reports of serious unrest in the city of 12 million, where wheat flour, available only at a few small mills, was selling for 16 rupees ($0.39) a kg, double its normal price.
"We are taking precautions to avoid disturbances as the situation seems explosive," said a police officer in Landhi.
On Thursday, thousands of people queued at big flour mills in Landhi, Korangi and other parts of Karachi, witnesses said.
They said some had looted trucks bringing wheat for grinding and that police had used batons in a charge on crowds which refused to leave flour mills empty handed. Police denied using batons.
Mill owners said about 3,000 bags of flour had been grabbed by angry crowds in the past three days.
"Our feast has been spoiled by the shortage," said one businessman on Friday after trying in vain to buy flour at a mill in the Pakistan Chowk area.
Many consumers switched to rice instead of bread to accompany the traditional feast on sheep and goats slaughtered in the streets on the first day of Eid al-Adha.
"Rice prices in retail stores have gone up slightly," a rice dealer said.
The wheat flour shortage, blamed on smuggling to war-ravaged Afghanistan, has hit the turbulent city of Karachi this week after affecting other parts of Pakistan earlier in the month.
Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif's government says the previous caretaker administration failed to arrange timely wheat imports.

Pakistan imported 1.8 million tonnes of wheat in July-March 1996/97 compared to 1.5 million in the year-ago period. A government official said on Thursday 472,500 tonnes of imported wheat would arrive by mid-May and no more imports were planned.
The government has set a wheat production target of 19 million tonnes for 1997/98 (July-June), compared to this year's harvest estimated at no more than 17 million tonnes.
